ORIGINAL ARTICLE

Engineering mechanics of bio-inspired architected cementitious materials (ACM) and composites (ACC) enabled by digital fabrication

Shashank Gupta . Reza Moini

Received: 1 June 2026 / Revised: 3 August 2026 / Accepted: 29 August 2026  The Author(s) 2026

Abstract Concrete is inherently weak and brittle under tension, making it susceptible to cracking under mechanical and environmental loading. Recent advances in digital fabrication enable control over spatial arrangements of cementitious materials across meso-to-macro length scales, shifting cementitious design from passively formed microstructures to intentionally engineered architecture. This review introduces two emerging classes of cementitious materials: architected cementitious materials (ACMs), formed by spatially arranging a single cementitious constituent (e.g., paste, mortar, concrete or ﬁber-reinforced counterparts), and architected cementitious composites (ACCs), formed by arranging multiple constituents such as concrete and polymer phases. We synthesize progress in bio-inspired ACMs and ACCs over the past decade, designed to improve mechanical and functional properties through digital and advanced manufacturing processes. Fundamental design principles, beyond mimicking geometry, inspired by several biological systems such as mantis shrimp, coelacanth ﬁsh scales, seashells, cortical bone, sea sponge, and nacre are discussed and pertinent engineered underlying (dissipative) toughening mechanisms are highlighted, including crack twisting, deﬂection, interlocking, arrest, renucleation and polymer bridging/deformation, and

tablet sliding. Key corresponding novel fabrication pathways enabling the design of ACMs and ACCs are highlighted, including 3D-printing, hybrid 3D-printing/casting, multi-material fabrication, and laser processing. Experimental, theoretical, and numerical approaches are synthesized to demonstrate how spatial arrangements and multi-materiality link design variables to toughening mechanisms. Key ﬁndings illucidate that controlled spatial arrangements and multimateriality enabled in ACMs and ACCs demonstrate a range of several-fold to two-orders-of-magnitude enhanced fracture toughness compared to conventional cement-based counterparts, while maintaining or improving ﬂexural strength. However, future progress requires resolving size effects, process-induced defects, reinforcement integration, and durability to enable scalable, high-performance ACMs and ACCs for infrastructure applications.

Whether concrete is viewed and studied as a material, a composite, or a structure (depending on its size and scale at which its mechanics is examined), there remains a need to address its fundamental ﬂaw: limited load-bearing capacity, crack resistance (i.e., fracture toughness), and brittleness under tension and bending [4, 5]. Whether arising from mechanical or environmental loading, cracking and damage tolerance and maintaining loadbearing upon fracture in conventional concrete are native challenges and matters of structural (in)efﬁ- ciency that need to be addressed, especially in response to the world’s growing population and accelerating urbanization with limited resources [6]. Although cementitious systems remain the foundation of modern infrastructure, their brittle or quasi-brittle response under tensile and ﬂexural loading [7–13] limits their ability to, in a stable manner, resist cracking, dissipate the stored strain energy, and maintain functionality and integrity after damage and fatigue cycles [14, 15] during crack initiation, coalescence, and propagation [16, 17]. In other words, while concrete as a structural material has proven to be a great cost-effective invention,itsdesignasacompositematerialhasremained pinned down by low tensile and fracture properties and hence has not substantially changed since its inception, exerting the need for steel reinforcement or bulk ﬁbers [2, 18]. Addressing these inherent limitations of concrete requires redeﬁning concrete as a material and adopting a new design thinking that allows for exploration and understanding of new forms of this ubiquitous material. Such an open perspective towards concrete, coupled with the advent of numerous advanced fabrication techniques, can enable harnessing new mechanics of concrete with higher mechanical efﬁciency while supporting more resilient infrastructure systems [2]. Recent advances in digital fabrication have introduced new opportunities to control the spatial arrangement, morphology, and placement of cementitious materials across multiple length scales [19, 20]. Approaches such as extrusion-based additive manufacturing [21–31], multi-material printing [32], hybrid 3D-printing and casting [33, 34], laser processing [35–37], lamination [35, 38], and powder-bed methods [39–41] provide new ways to organize material and space across different length scales. These emerging manufacturing capabilities make it possible to move beyond monolithic cementitious

systems toward steadily growing architected classes of cementitious materials and composites, where mechanical performance can be engineered, enhanced, and tuned through designed arrangements and multimateriality degrees of freedom, rather than microstructural composition alone [2]. Here, these material systems are broadly classiﬁed into two categories:

• Architected cementitious materials (ACMs): Cement-based materials with purposeful design of spatial arrangements of a single constituent material at the mesoscale, engineered to deliberately control, tailor, or enhance targeted mechanical response and properties that are unattainable through monolithic counterparts. • Architected cementitious composites (ACCs): Cement-based composites with purposeful design of spatial arrangements of two or more distinct constituent materials at the mesoscale, engineered to achieve targeted mechanical responses and properties that are unattainable through monolithic counterparts.

2 Bio-inspired design motifs and toughening mechanisms for engineering mechanics

Human-made engineering materials, including cementitious materials, often exhibit trade-offs among key mechanical properties, particularly strength and fracture toughness [62, 63]. This mutual exclusivity

arises because the mechanisms that increase strength commonly restrict deformation and damage dissipation, while mechanisms that enhance toughness often rely on inelastic deformation, crack deﬂection, or energy-dissipating processes [62]. As a result, the development of mutually strong, tough, damagetolerant (cementitious) materials has remained a major challenge at the material’s mechanics level, leading to structural design inefﬁciencies, which has traditionally involved a compromise between load-bearing capacity and resistance to fracture at large scale [62]. Biological materials provide a compelling source of inspiration for overcoming such trade-offs. Many evolved materials exhibit unprecedented combinations of strength, stiffness, toughness, and damage tolerance despite being composed of a limited set of constituents [64, 65]. Rather than relying on intrinsically superior materials, nature often achieves these properties through purposeful spatial and morphological arrangements across micro- and nanoscale length scales, including controlled organization of material, pores, and hard and soft phases [65]. Translating these arrangements into a growing body of literature on ACMs and ACCs provides a pathway to engineer cementitious materials with improved fracture resistance and damage tolerance. Biomimicry can take place in various forms and levels. One of the fundamental approaches to bioinspired design is to not merely replicate the geometries or spatial morphologies, but rather to engineer the underlying mechanisms that exist in the biological source in order to enable the resulting function. The Bouligand architecture present in the mantis shrimp dactyl club consists of parallel chitin ﬁbril sheets embedded in a protein matrix and stacked in a helicoidal pattern (Fig. 3a) [76, 77]. The relative rotation between adjacent sheets is commonly described by a pitch angle (c), which deﬁnes the gradual twisting of the ﬁbril orientation through the thickness [76, 77]. This arrangement can promote a crack twisting toughening mechanism by forcing an advancing crack to rotate through successive layers rather than propagate along a straight path (Fig. 3a). The double-Bouligand architecture, observed in ﬁsh scales such as those of coelacanth ﬁsh, extends this concept through orthogonal bi-layer units (Fig. 3b) [78]. In this architecture, ﬁbrils in one sheet are coupled perpendicular to those in the adjacent sheet, forming a bi-layer that rotates progressively through the thickness. The pitch angle (c) similarly deﬁnes the relative rotation between neighboring bi-layer units, producing a double-helical arrangement analogous to

the single-Bouligand motif [28, 78]. When translated into ACMs, Bouligand arrangements promote crack twisting and interlocking toughening mechanisms, whereas double-Bouligand arrangements combine crack twisting, interlocking, and bi-layer shielding to improve fracture toughness (Fig. 3a, b) [28]. The Sinusoidal architecture, present in the shell of Saxidomus purpuratus, provides another bio-inspired motif for ACMs (Fig. 3c) [79]. Depending on the sinusoidal orientation and amplitude, cracks may deﬂect along the printed interfaces or penetrate through the ﬁlaments when interfacial deﬂection is no longer energetically favorable. In Y- and Z-sinusoidal ACMs, the undulating geometry can also generate non-uniform stress distributions, with tensile stresses concentrating near sinusoidal troughs and inﬂuencing the location of crack initiation (Fig. 3c) [29]. These mechanisms provide a pathway for improving fracture response and ﬂexural strength through perturbed stress distribution and a kinked crack plane [29]. Cortical bone offers another bio-inspired strategy for designing damage-tolerant ACMs (Fig. 3d). In the human femur, the dense cortical region contains tubular osteons, or Haversian systems, embedded within an organic matrix [80, 81]. These osteons surround Haversian canals and are encircled by cement lines, which act as mechanically weaker interfaces compared with the surrounding mineralized tissue [87]. Because of this mechanical contrast, propagating cracks tend to interact with the osteon structure and deviate from a straight path, leading to crack-cement line interactions and crack deﬂection toughening mechanisms around the tubular features [80, 81]. When translated into cementitious materials, such tubular arrangements provide a strategy for introducing controlled crack-tubular heterogeneity interactions, enabling non-abrupt fracture behavior and enhanced energy dissipation in cortical boneinspired ACMs (Fig. 3d) [34]. Biological materials, such as cortical bone and dentin, often exhibit inherent disorder in their designs, including variations in shape, size, orientation, and distribution of architected features [34]. Disorder can act as an additional design feature, offering inspiration for advanced architected materials with improved damage tolerance. Recent work has used a statistical-mechanicsbased approach to quantify disorder in biological designs and tubular ACMs. In cortical bone-inspired tubular ACMs, radial distribution functions and order parameters (translational and orientational) were used to quantify the degree of disorder [34]. The statisticalmechanics-based approach provides a quantitative pathway to study design-property relationships in concrete and bio-inspired ACMs and ACCs.

The sea sponge provides another bio-inspired model for designing layered hard-soft ACCs (Fig. 3e). Euplectella aspergillum, commonly known as the Venus ﬂower basket, is a deep-sea glass sponge whose skeletal system maintains mechanical resilience despite being primarily composed of brittle silica [82, 83]. Its spicules consist of a central organic ﬁlament surrounded by alternating concentric layers of silica nanoparticles and thin organic phases between the layers [82, 83]. This hard-soft layered arrangement provides a natural design strategy for combining stiff cementitious layers with compliant polymeric phases in ACCs [32]. When translated into cementitious composites, the resulting layered hardsoft arrangement can promote toughening mechanisms, including crack arrest and deﬂection, partial debonding, crack bridging, load transfer after local damage, and energy dissipation, thereby enabling multi-stage fracture, controlled post-peak softening, and enhanced fracture toughness and ductility (Fig. 3e) [32]. Natural nacre provides a well-established bioinspired brick-and-mortar design strategy for ACCs (Fig. 3f) [35, 38, 46, 88]. It consists of stiff polygonal aragonite tablets arranged in layered sheets and separated by a thin, compliant biopolymer matrix, forming a three-dimensional brick-and-mortar arrangement [84, 89]. Despite being composed primarily of brittle aragonite, nacre achieves high toughness, strength, and ductility through the coordinated interaction between its hard tablets and soft organic phases [84, 85]. When translated into cementitious composites, this arrangement motivates the use of cementitious tablets or layers combined with compliant polymeric phases [35, 38, 88]. The resulting nacre-like ACCs can promote several effective toughening mechanisms, including tablet sliding, interlayer deformation, crack deﬂection, bridging, and energy dissipation, thereby enhancing fracture toughness and ductility while delaying catastrophic failure (Fig. 3f) [35]. The uniqueness of a mechanistic approach to bioinspired design is the ability to both understand and engineer properties from a fundamental perspective rather than attempting to replicate the geometric motifs of natural systems. This is a more effective approach for guiding the design and development of ACMs and ACCs with actively tunable properties and for engineering the properties of concrete as a

3 ACM/ACC-enabling digital fabrication techniques

Progress in controlling spatial and multi-material arrangements in ACMs and ACCs over the past decade has been strongly enabled by advances in digital fabrication across length scales, from small laboratory-scale specimens to large structural components. These developments include direct extrusionbased methods [21–29, 31] that enable the fabrication of relatively complex geometries; hybrid approaches that combine 3D-printed molds with conventional casting [33, 34]; multi-material additive manufacturing strategies capable of depositing materials with distinct properties in a programmable manner [32]; and laser-processing techniques for cutting or grooving cementitious materials according to prescribed designs, often in combination with lamination processes [35, 36, 38]. Collectively, these fabrication strategies have expanded the design space for ACMs and ACCs over the past decade, enabling the realization of bespoke geometries and new approaches for achieving controlled spatial and morphological arrangements in these materials. In particular, extrusion-based additive manufacturing has played a central role in the development of ACMs due to its relative simplicity, adaptability, and applicability across length scales compared with other digital fabrication methods (Fig. 4a). At the millimeter scale, benchtop systems such as a reconﬁgured commercial polymer 3D-printer (as demonstrated in Fig. 4a) [27, 90, 91], with nozzle sizes in the order of  a few mm, have enabled rapid prototyping and experimental studies of cement paste-based ACMs, including Bouligand and tubular designs. At the centimeter scale, mid-size systems such as the SCARA robotic system [29, 92, 93], with larger nozzle sizes of several to  10 mm, have supported the transition from cement paste to mortar, enabling larger-scale ACMs such as sinusoidal designs. At the meter scale, robotic and gantry-based systems, with nozzle sizes of  10s of mm, have enabled the

fabrication of ACMs at dimensions closer to and more relevant to infrastructure components scale. Figure 4a highlights a two-component (2-K) robotic extrusion platform that enables near-real-time control of material rheology by accelerating or decelerating hydration at the nozzle [22, 28]. Unlike single-component systems based on continuous mixing and pumping, this approach combines dry powder feeding, staged mixing and pumping, and secondary agitation within a nozzle-mounted chamber, where liquid-phase admixtures such as accelerators can be introduced. This localized control over rheology and hydration, particularly when coupled with sensing and monitoring capabilities, provides a pathway for fabricating complex, structural-scale ACMs such as Bouligand and double-Bouligand designs (Fig. 4a). Another approach involves hybrid 3D-printing and casting [33, 34], which provides an effective strategy for fabricating ACMs with controlled spatial features (Fig. 4b). In this process, a positive mold is ﬁrst 3Dprinted using a dissolvable polymer, such as polyvinyl alcohol (PVA). A two-component urethane rubber is then poured into the printed mold to form a ﬂexible negative mold, with vacuum degassing used to remove entrapped air before curing. After hardening, the PVA mold is dissolved, leaving behind the urethane mold. Fresh cementitious material is subsequently cast into this mold to produce the desired ACM, such as the tubular design exhibited in Fig. 4b, followed by controlled curing. This hybrid strategy combines the geometric freedom of polymer 3D printing with the ﬁdelity of cementitious casting, enabling the fabrication of architected specimens with controlled internal and external features. Multi-material additive manufacturing has emerged most recently and provides a powerful strategy for fabricating ACCs by enabling the controlled deposition of materials with distinct properties within a single printed structure (Fig. 4c) [32, 94, 95]. Custom multi-material platforms can integrate different extrusion-based processes, such as fused ﬁlament fabrication, direct ink writing, and elastomer or polymer extrusion, with each deposition mode tailored to the rheological and processing requirements of the constituent materials [32, 95]. This capability is transformative, as it allows cementitious, polymeric, and elastomeric phases to be spatially programmed at the mesoscale, enabling layered, interlaced, lamellar, or hybrid ACC designs, as presented in Fig. 4c

By controlling the placement and interaction of phases with contrasting stiffness, strength, ductility, or energy-dissipation capacity, multi-material printing offers a direct pathway for engineering mechanical functionality in architected cementitious composites. Laser-processing (i.e., engraving or tabulating) combined with lamination offers another strategy for fabricating bio-inspired ACCs, such as nacre-like composites (Fig. 4d) [35, 36, 96]. In this approach, cement paste sheets are ﬁrst patterned using laser processing to create controlled grooves or, when desired, to separate them into tablet-like units. The processed sheets are then assembled through a layerby-layer lamination process in which a soft polymeric interlayer, such as PVS, is introduced between successive cementitious layers. Each layer is aligned and lightly pressed to promote contact and adhesion, producing a staggered multilayer ACC that mimics the tablet-and-mortar arrangement of natural nacre. This approach enables control over tablet geometry, interlayer thickness, and spatial organization within the composite. Together, these digital fabrication strategies provide broad opportunities for producing ACMs and ACCs across multiple length scales, from small-scale prototypes for fundamental studies to larger components approaching infrastructure-relevant dimensions, and from architected materials toward architected structures. The ability to probe architected designs across this scale range is essential for studying, reﬁning, and maturing well-characterized material systems for future deployment. In this context, progress in architected infrastructure materials can be understood through the combined evolution of materials, fabrication processes, achievable scales, and targeted mechanical functions. Despite these enabling manufacturing opportunities, each fabrication route has some limitations. In extrusion-based additive manufacturing, the printable mix design should balance ﬂowability, extrudability, shape retention, and buildability, with earlyage deformation strongly linked to rheological properties and solids content [26, 91, 97, 98]. Micro-CT and SEM-based studies have demonstrated that extrusion-based 3D-printing creates interfacial regions with distinct pore structure and connectivity compared with cast counterparts [24, 36, 90, 99, 100]. These interfaces may act as defects, but in ACMs and ACCs they can also be intentionally used as architected

features to guide crack propagation and activate toughening mechanisms [27, 36]. At larger scales, extrusion-based additive manufacturing also remains limited by reinforcement integration, process control, geometric ﬁdelity, and ﬁnish quality [101–103]. Other fabrication approaches face other constraints. Hybrid 3D-printing/casting can produce controlled internal features but often requires sacriﬁcial molds, negative molds, dissolution, degassing, and casting steps, making the process indirect and potentially less scalable for large or highly customized components [34, 104]. Multi-material AM (MMA) enables programmable hard-soft ACCs; however, it requires compatible interfacial properties between dissimilar phases [32, 33]. Laser-processing and lamination provide high geometric control for nacre-like ACCs, but laser groove depth and notch quality depend on laser power and scanning conditions, and local heating can generate melting, redeposition, and damage around the groove region [36, 37, 96, 105]. Lamination also depends on accurate layer alignment, control of interlayer thickness, and reliable adhesion between layers; therefore, manual assembly can become challenging for larger specimens or components [35, 46, 71]. Building on these fabrication foundation pathways, the next generation of bio-inspired ACMs and ACCs designs are ought to be mechanics-informed in order to fundamentally and mutually improve load-bearing and fracture response at a large scale. The next section elaborates on how controlled spatial and morphological arrangements are used to engineer toughening mechanisms, enhance toughness, and promote damage-tolerant behavior at the meso scale and can inform the future developments at a large scale.

Together, these observations indicate that the mechanical beneﬁt of Bouligand and double- Bouligand arrangements depends on the combined effects of pitch angle, ﬁlament orientation, interface conﬁguration, and loading direction. One representative example is demonstrated in Fig. 5a, where Bouligand and double-Bouligand ACMs fabricated by two-component robotic additive manufacturing were compared with parallel lamellar and monolithic cast references [28]. Under SENB loading, the Bouligand, double-Bouligand, lamellar, and cast specimens exhibited comparable peak loads, but their post-peak responses differed markedly. The cast and lamellar specimens failed in a brittle manner, whereas the Bouligand and double-Bouligand ACMs showed post-peak softening and more stable crack growth, leading to higher fracture toughness than the cast reference [28]. The improved fracture response was attributed to crack twisting, bi-layer crack shielding, and interlocking [16]. In the double-Bouligand ACMs, cracks deﬂected along alternating interfaces and through bilayer ﬁlaments across multiple printed layers, producing a tortuous fracture surface and promoting interlocking behind the crack tip. These mechanisms delayed unstable fracture and increased the energy required for crack propagation [28].

4.4 Nacre-like and hard-soft layered ACCs

Layered ACCs have been developed using different hard cementitious and soft hyperelastic phases to improve fracture resistance, ductility, and energy absorption, as presented in Table 3 [32, 35, 46, 71, 72]. The hard phases include cement paste [35], mortar [32], ECC [71], geopolymer paste [72], and steel-bar array frame-reinforced concrete (SBRC) [46], while the soft phases include hyperelastic polymers, including polyvinyl siloxane (PVS) [35], silicone (SI) [32], polyurethane (PU) [32, 46, 71], and polymers with different stiffness [72]. Fabrication methods range from laser processing and lamination [32, 35, 46, 71, 72], multi-material additive manufacturing (MMAM) [32], casting followed by manual assembly [71], and bottom-up assembly [46]. The tested beam specimens range from 110 to 300 mm in length or span, while larger steel–concrete target blocks reach 300 9 300 9 300 mm [32, 35, 46, 71, 72]. Most layered ACC studies used quasi-static 3 PB and SENB tests to evaluate ﬂexural strength, fracture toughness, fracture energy, or speciﬁc J-integral [32, 35, 46, 71, 72]. The reported quasi-static displacement rates range from 0.05 to 0.5 mm/min. Here, two examples are discussed in detail, including auxetic cementitious cellular composites and triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) based ACMs/ACCs. Auxetic cementitious cellular composites can be deﬁned as a type of ACM because they consist of one cementitious constituent material (e.g., concrete, SHCC, etc.) and have been developed using a hybrid 3D-printing/casting process, also described as additive-manufacturing-assisted casting, to introduce controlled cellular void architectures such as peanutshaped and elliptical auxetic unit cells [104, 131–133]. By engineering the spatial arrangement of voids, these materials broaden the design space of digitally fabricated cementitious systems toward negative Poisson’s ratio behavior, energy dissipation, and impact resistance [104, 131–133]. In this sense, auxetic cementitious cellular composites can be viewed as a broader extension of bone-inspired tubular ACMs, where void geometry and spatial arrangement are used not only to interact with cracks but also to program deformation, strain distribution, and energy absorption. Representative studies in the literature, such as those examining energy dissipation under impact, have combined DIC-based major strain ﬁelds with numerical simulations of maximum principal plastic strain, as presented in Fig. 8a [131]. These results demonstrate that elliptical auxetic void arrangements distribute deformation across multiple ligaments and promote energy dissipation, whereas the circular reference design exhibits more localized deformation beneath the impactor [131]. The transition from circular to elliptical void arrangements induces auxetic behavior in the auxetic cementitious cellular composites, enabling greater endurance under repeated impacts and higher accumulated energy absorption before failure [131]. TPMS geometries are another examples where the architected arrangement provides a route for expanding the design space of digitally fabricated ACMs and ACCs. These geometries are also motivated by biological TPMS-like porous structures, including the stereom of sea urchin spines [74] and the ossicles of knobby starﬁsh [75], which demonstrate how continuous cellular mineral networks can provide lightweight structural support and damage tolerance. 5 Summary and conclusion

Bio-inspired ACMs and ACCs are two emerging classes of materials that provide new opportunities to rethink the design and engineering the properties of cement paste, mortar, and concrete beyond their conventional brittle or quasi-brittle tensile response. In principle, the concept expands beyond cementitious materials into other brittle and quasi-brittle construction materials and binders (including sustainable binders). By introducing spatial architecture in ACMs and multi-material arrangements in ACCs as additional design degrees of freedom, these systems broaden the deﬁnition of concrete and expand its mechanical and functional performance toward improved damage resilience, ductility, toughness, and multifunctionality. This review crystallizes how underlying biological design motifs and mechanisms, informed by the fundamental mechanics of solids, and enabled by digital fabrication strategies come together to engineer the next generation of high-performance cementitious materials in form of ACM and ACC systems. ACMs and ACCs, inspired by the intricate arrangements in several evolved biological materials are reviewed including mantis shrimp dactyl club [28], ﬁsh scales [28], cortical bone [34], bivalve shells [29], abalone nacre [35, 139], sea-sponges [32], and human skull [22, 47]. In the ACM class, the developments have led to novel double-helical [28], tubular [34], sinusoidal [29], and cellular [21] architected arrangements. In the ACC class, novel arrangements including novel tabulated brick-and-mortar [35], layered hard-soft (concrete-hyperelastic polymers) [32], and interlocking suture hard-soft composites [47]. These ACM and ACC designs have resulted in a range of several fold

to two-orders-of-magnitude improved fracture toughness [32, 35], as represented along the vertical axis of Fig. 7, while maintaining or improving speciﬁc ﬂexural strength [28, 29, 32], as demonstrated along the horizontal axis of Fig. 7. At the same time, ACM and ACC have reported to improve ductility by over oneorder-of-magnitude in some cases [32, 35]. Additional property-design relationships, including improvements in energy absorption, impact and penetration resistance, compressive strength, and various forms of damage tolerance, are summarized for ACMs and ACCs in Tables 2 and 3, respectively. More importantly, a plethora of underlying toughening mechanisms present in biological systems are discussed and have been engineered in concrete materials to date, as observed across the six biological systems considered in this review, such as crack twisting, shielding, and interlocking in helical architecture [28]; crack kinking due to stress concentration in sinusoidal architecture [29]; crack arrest and renucleation by engineered defects in tubular architecture [34]; crack tortuosity through tablet sliding in brick-and-mortar nacre-like architecture [35]; and crack arrest, re-nucleation, bridging, and tension/ shear-dominated interfacial damage in layered hardsoft architecture [32]. In short, the resulting damage delocalization, multiple crack fronts, and enlarged fracture process zone achieved by engineering these toughening mechanisms across ACMs and ACCs have enabled substantial improvements in fracture toughness, ductility, energy dissipation, and damage tolerance as high as one-order-of-magnitude in some cases. The signiﬁcance of developing ACMs and ACCs is that they can: (i) overcome the limited microstructural toughening mechanisms in cement-based materials (e.g., aggregate bridging, micro-cracking) by engineering a wide range of toughening mechanisms through meso-scale architecture; (ii) open an entirely new approach to improve the fracture response of brittle and quasi-brittle materials under tension and bending similar to those in composite structures; and (iii) address the most fundamental shortcomings of concrete as a structural material, which are poor resistance to fracture/cracking, limited energy dissipation, and brittle response, moving toward more damage-resilient and structurally efﬁcient design. By learning from mutual inclusivity in natural materials, the research on bio-inspired architectures at

As ACMs and ACCs exert greater control over the mechanical responses of concrete while retaining existing advantages, such architected approach to design can be expanded at the macro scale and help transform concrete into tougher, longer-lasting, structurally efﬁcient infrastructure solutions. Lastly, digital fabrication provides important design degrees of freedom for translating bio-inspired motifs into ACMs and ACCs, including control over ﬁlament placement, orientation, spacing, interfaces, phase distribution, and meso-scale to macroscale morphology. 6 Future directions and approaches

Despite this progress, the design space of bio-inspired ACMs and ACCs and non-bio-inspired counterparts remains only partially explored. In the future, two bio-inspired approaches can broadly be envisioned beyond mimicking shapes and geometries: (1) identifying gaps in engineering (cementitious) materials and investigating solutions in natural organisms and systems, and most important the underlying mechanisms that can address the bottlenecks in their engineering counterparts, and (2) Identifying natural materials with inspiring geomtries and underlying mechanisms, properties, or function and engineering their utility into an engineered (cementitious) counterparts depending on the properties and application of interest. While nature is hierarchical, in the future, focusing on one scale and one mechanism at a time allows for more rigorous scientiﬁc exploration of the examined phenomena, from which global behaviors and mechanics can emerge. In terms of engineering mechanics, approaches that systematically connect design variables with fracture toughness, strength, ductility, energy dissipation, and other mechanical or functional properties are worthwhile efforts to pave the groundwork for future emerging behaviors.

Fracture mechanics remains an under-utilized ﬁeld when it comes to design of architected materials and composites. It provides a powerful fundamental tool for the study of non-linear phenomena in cementitious materials and developing mechanistic design strategies. Such efforts, when coupled with rapid prototyping at a small scale, can help quickly probe the large design variable space and identify the most effective designs approach to design for further investigation under certain loading conditions and performance objectives. Because ACMs and ACCs involve coupled choices of spatial arrangement, constituent materials, and interfacial properties, future theoretical, computational, and data-driven approaches can accelerate exploration of this broad design space. Analytical and numerical models can evaluate how constituent materials, interfaces, and geometric imperfections affect the response of a wide range of architected designs, while optimization [140, 141] and machinelearning approaches [142, 143] can help identify architected designs suited for enhancing toughness, maintaining strength, improving ductility, or enabling multifunctional performance. An important future opportunity is the deliberate design of heterogeneity through its quantiﬁcation. Spatial arrangement cannot be properly designed if it cannot be quantiﬁed, in particular in ACMs and ACCs. Recent transformative work has proposed to quantify disorder in architected materials using statisticalmechanics-based functions and scalar descriptors, such as radial distribution functions and order parameters [34], moving beyond simple classiﬁcations such as periodic or non-periodic arrangements [133, 144–147]. Future studies can build on this direction by quantifying broader disorder spectra in connection to design. This connection has remained largely not well-understood across both conventional concrete and biological materials. Furthermore, the majority of the current bio-inspired ACM and ACC design-property investigations have remained at the lab-scale, with reported specimen sizes up to several hundred mm [28]. Past studies are limited to selected loading orientations, mode-I loading, or monotonic quasi-static tests; therefore, orientation dependence, multiaxial response, cyclic loading, and impact performance require further investigation for several ACM and ACC systems [28, 29, 32, 34, 35, 46, 71, 72]. Future work should also address size effects and fabrication challenges, including processinduced heterogeneities, geometric ﬁdelity, reinforcement integration, long-term durability of polymeric phases, environmental exposure, ﬁre resistance, durability assessment such as freeze–thaw resistance, and standardization before infrastructure-scale implementation [24, 26, 32, 35, 97, 99, 101, 102]. Beyond material and testing limitations, practical implementation also requires reliable translation of complex architectures into manufacturable toolpaths. Future progress will therefore depend on accessible design tools, automated toolpath-generation methods [148], and fabrication workﬂows that connect architected material concepts to practical ACM and ACC production. Lastly, future progress will require scaling both design and fabrication strategies to translate these architected designs into high-quality, realizable, performance-driven cementitious systems for demanding infrastructure applications, including damage-resilient and degradation-resistant components, as well as more advanced multi-functional structural elements and systems.
